content.short_compare_copy: Type 5, The Investigator first tracks information, boundaries, resource demands, and complete understanding; Type 9, The Peacemaker first tracks overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm. Compare the sequence in one real setting without forcing a choice.
content.resonance_feedback_prompt: Mark only observations supported by an event record or another person’s feedback. Familiarity, preference, and a single behavior cannot decide between Type 5, The Investigator and Type 9, The Peacemaker.
content.shared_surface_similarity: When the issue is complex, viewpoints diverge, and discussion will not close, Type 5, The Investigator and Type 9, The Peacemaker may both look invested, alert, or willing to take responsibility. The useful distinction is whether attention first moves toward information, boundaries, resource demands, and complete understanding or overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm.
content.seven_day_observation_question: For seven days, record three events resembling “the issue is complex, viewpoints diverge, and discussion will not close. ” Did the first cue, first action, and later cost fit information, boundaries, resource demands, and complete understanding or overall stability, other viewpoints, conflict cost, and familiar rhythm more closely? Keep one event that neither candidate explains well.

actions.title: Time-box research and release the draft
actions.instruction: Set a deadline and minimum output format for a task still under research. Release a draft at that time, label unknowns, and stop substituting further collection for output.
actions.observable_outcome: Record what was known at release, the effect of omissions, and how much feedback-driven revision followed. Identify which extra preparation would actually have mattered.

actions.title: Share one unfinished thought before full preparation
actions.instruction: Before feeling fully prepared, share one developing view with a trusted person. Label it as provisional and specify the kind of feedback you want.
actions.observable_outcome: Track tension around incompleteness, the quality of information received, and whether exchange made the view more accurate rather than less controlled.

actions.title: State capacity and availability in advance
actions.instruction: Before energy is depleted, state your available time, present capacity, and next response point. Do not wait for withdrawal or silence to communicate the boundary.
actions.observable_outcome: Check whether others adjusted the request, whether recovery became predictable, and whether the limit was clear instead of abruptly closed.

actions.title: Ask one live question instead of modeling alone
actions.instruction: For one complex problem, ask a relevant person a single question before analyzing alone. Target missing information rather than presenting the whole model.
actions.observable_outcome: Record analysis time saved or added, any false assumption exposed, and whether the resource cost of direct contact matched the forecast.

actions.title: Schedule one brief period of real-time participation
actions.instruction: Schedule one ten-minute instance of live participation each day: speak, work alongside someone, or remain briefly present. Bound the duration and do not immediately compensate with extra isolation.
actions.observable_outcome: Compare predicted and actual energy cost, one piece of information gained, and one reason personal space still mattered. Use both sides to calibrate the boundary.

actions.title: State your preference first in one small decision
actions.instruction: Each day, state your preference first in one small decision, including the option and timing, before hearing others. Do not withdraw it with “anything is fine. ”
actions.observable_outcome: Record response time, the other person’s actual reaction, and the final choice. Test whether difference truly damaged connection.

actions.title: Put the most important task in the first work block
actions.instruction: Place the most important task in the first available block and close one habitual activity before starting. Require only a minimum advance rather than the right overall mood.
actions.observable_outcome: Compare progress, reduction in routine activity, and energy. Identify the trigger that most often removes the priority from view.

actions.title: Set a firm deadline for one delayed decision
actions.instruction: For one delayed decision, set a date, required information, and a default option at expiry. Once information is sufficient, do not use further coordination to postpone choice.
actions.observable_outcome: Record whether the deadline held, the cost of delay, and unresolved disagreement. Allow only one replacement date with a written reason.

actions.title: Restate what you genuinely agree to before saying yes
actions.instruction: Before agreeing, repeat what you will own, what you will not own, and what the other person must carry. Wait for confirmation before beginning.
actions.observable_outcome: Check whether the commitment stayed clear, whether resentment or forgetting decreased, and whether you expanded scope merely to restore harmony.

actions.title: Record one disagreement that the relationship survived
actions.instruction: Track the twenty-four hours after voicing one disagreement: the response, relationship change, and issue progress. Do not use immediate tension to predict permanent rupture.
actions.observable_outcome: Compare expected and actual consequences, keeping evidence of continued stability alongside facts that require repair or a renewed boundary.

actions.title: Correct one material issue and defer the rest
actions.instruction: Choose a reversible task with several visible flaws. Rank them by material risk, correct only the first, place the rest on tomorrow’s list, and stop at the criterion set in advance.
actions.observable_outcome: Record whether deferred issues caused harm, how long delivery took, and whether physical tension eased after stopping. If material risk grew, revise the risk rule instead of forcing the exercise.

actions.title: Ask what risk the other person sees before stating the standard
actions.instruction: Before stating a standard, ask what risk the other person sees and summarize the answer in one sentence. Then separate required correction from personal preference.
actions.observable_outcome: Note any information you had missed, whether the discussion reached a shared standard sooner, and whether you still expressed the boundary clearly.

actions.title: Define “good enough” for one low-risk task
actions.instruction: Before a low-risk task, define minimum acceptance, one risk that must be controlled, and two details that may remain unfinished. Deliver when those conditions are met without raising the bar afterward.
actions.observable_outcome: Compare the written standard with the outcome, any rework, and whether others could use the result. Mark which feared imperfections never became consequential.

actions.title: Observe one acceptable outcome after choosing not to correct immediately
actions.instruction: Leave one safe, repairable imperfection untouched for twenty-four hours. Record each urge to correct it and the reason without suppressing the discomfort.
actions.observable_outcome: After twenty-four hours, check the actual consequence, attention consumed, and other people’s responses. If the issue mattered, document the evidence rather than calling the exercise a failure.

actions.title: Turn one criticism into a specific request
actions.instruction: Take one recent criticism and rewrite it as an observable fact, its impact, and a bounded request. Leave room for a response without adding a moral judgment.
actions.observable_outcome: Keep the original and revised versions, then note whether the request could be answered, whether conflict intensity changed, and whether it addressed a material risk.

steps.prompt: Today, just choose a scene that makes you noticeably tense, want to push forward, want to explain, want to get closer, want to control, or want to move away. Write what happened and what you did first, without rushing to analyze the numbers.

Think back to an uncomfortable moment today: Did you care more about being right, recognized, needed, safe, bounded, free, true expression, or calm? Choose only the closest one and write a sentence of evidence.

No need to stereotype yourself. Just look back at the first three days: Which type of motivation appears slightly more often in the clues? If it's not clear, choose it unclearly and write down a real scene that you can look back on.

Today, observe the first step after stress arises: fight, explain, retreat, please, transfer, control, numb, find someone to confirm, or something else? Only record the first step and how to recover later.

Choose a relationship with minor friction and record whether you would rather be understood, recognized, have boundaries respected, promised, needed, or let the situation settle down. Just write about your own needs and behaviors.

Just look at one less natural resource today: asking for help, saying no, expressing anger, relaxing and enjoying, acknowledging a need, establishing rules, showing initiative, stopping to feel, or taking on conflict.

Look back on the week and don't ask which number was better, just which explanations are more relevant to your daily motivations. You can choose Top1, Top2, Top3, Others or Still Not Sure, and write a sentence of evidence that can be reviewed.

sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to information, boundaries, resource use, and completeness of understanding.
sections.title: The overall pattern
points: Repeatedly noticing information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding supports this candidate more than one isolated behavior.
If genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion explains the pattern better, a stable type hypothesis deserves less weight.
paragraphs: When information is incomplete, boundaries are unclear, or requests expand suddenly, you may step back to understand the system and its resource cost before participating. Quietness and love of learning are less specific than making understanding and space prerequisites for action.

Distance can protect capability and control over energy, but introversion, fatigue, and specialist roles can look similar. Repeatedly learning through participation before full preparation would moderate this candidate.
sections.reflection_question: Recall one episode when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks. Where did your attention go first? What supports this candidate, and what points instead to the counterexample that you can take a first step before the picture is complete?

sections.lead: You may notice information, boundaries, resource use, and completeness of understanding earlier than people around you and allocate effort from there.
sections.title: What draws attention and what you protect
points: The first object of attention can reveal an effort to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn.
Test that possibility against actual trade-offs while ruling out genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion.
paragraphs: When a new request arrives, you may estimate its information, time, and contact demands before opening resources. Boundary and completeness of understanding shape participation together.

Learning through participation despite incomplete information shows that space is not an absolute prerequisite. Endless preparation before entering the setting strengthens the resource-protection hypothesis.
sections.reflection_question: In a situation when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, what were you trying hardest to preserve? Which observable consequences help separate necessary preparation from delayed participation?

sections.lead: The visible move may be to observe, model, and conserve before entering once preparation feels sufficient; the less spoken need may be to retain space and competence while trusting that learning can continue through participation.
sections.title: Outer expression and the need beneath it
points: The visible move may be to step back, gather knowledge, and enter later; its purpose still requires contextual and first-person evidence.
Even when the aim is to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn, another person’s reported impact remains independent evidence.
paragraphs: Under pressure, you may withdraw, gather information, reduce expression, delay commitment, or tighten boundaries. That can protect concentration, but it can also reduce useful feedback and connection. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis.
Quiet, delayed response, or a need for space may be read as disinterest. Treat that as a communication hypothesis and make the timing and scope of your return visible.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks in which someone saw your behavior but may not have understood its purpose. What did you hope to protect, and what alternative explanation did their response add?

sections.lead: A possible habitual sequence is to feel intruded upon, withdraw to gather more information, and become less familiar with the live situation.
sections.title: How emotion reinforces the habitual loop
points: A loop around information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding narrows through interpretation, emotion, and action rather than appearing all at once.
The pause before you step back, gather knowledge, and enter later is the point where another response may still be available.
paragraphs: Possible pressure cues include being overdrawn, expected to respond immediately, asked to decide with incomplete information, or having private space interrupted. The report cannot determine what you fear or equate a need for preparation with incapacity.
Early signals may include increasingly delayed replies, information gathering without a stopping rule, discussions that stay entirely analytical, or heightened sensitivity to requests.
sections.reflection_question: The last time when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, in what order did emotion, interpretation, and action occur? If you paused at the second step, what different response would still have been available?

sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that introversion, research habits, or temporary depletion can resemble a stable resource-defense pattern.
sections.title: How to recognize the pattern without mistyping
points: Attention to information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding across work, relationships, and private choices carries more weight than behavior in one role.
Keep genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion as a serious competing explanation.
paragraphs: You may interpret ‘I am not fully prepared’ as ‘I cannot participate yet.’ Look for a smaller contribution that is honest about uncertainty and still creates contact with reality.

If Type 5 does not become the main clue this time, you can think of it as a low-use resource hypothesis: observe whether you are less active in using analysis, blank space, and knowledge organization to restore clarity when the information is incomplete, boundaries are squeezed, or independent judgment is needed. It’s not judging you as irrational or lacking in understanding.
sections.reflection_question: When distinguishing necessary preparation from delayed participation, which evidence repeats across settings, and which similar behavior is better explained by role, culture, temporary strain, or a learned habit?

sections.lead: Type 5, The Investigator is adjacent to Type 4, The Individualist and Type 6, The Loyalist. Adjacency theory supports comparison, but a second-place score or one behavior cannot determine a wing.
sections.title: How to read adjacent-type influences
points: Adjacent types: 4 and 6
Second place is not a wing assignment
Use longitudinal situations and counterexamples without assigning arrows, subtype, or level
paragraphs: Compare the recurring attention behind information, boundaries, resource use, and completeness of understanding with what each adjacent type protects; do not convert ranking into identity.
Arrows, wings, subtypes, and development levels remain theory-reading layers. This result reports only relative distribution within one form.
sections.reflection_question: If a neighboring type also resonates, which core concern better explains your trade-offs when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks? What evidence is still missing before treating a wing as more than a theory prompt?

sections.lead: With enough capacity, this pattern may help you decompose complex systems, identify decisive variables, and preserve independent judgment.
sections.title: How the pattern helps when capacity is available
points: With enough capacity, attention to information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding can become a concrete contribution.
A resourceful expression can prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn while leaving room for other methods.
paragraphs: With more capacity and choice, when judgment needs to pause, you may stay clear enough to sort information without being carried by the first emotional signal.
When judgment needs to pause, you may stay clear enough to sort information without being carried by the first emotional signal.
sections.reflection_question: In one situation when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks where you still had enough capacity, whom did this attention pattern help and what problem did it solve? Which condition made it a resource rather than an automatic response?

sections.lead: When flexibility drops, the same tendency may make preparation a prerequisite for contact so knowledge grows while participation recedes.
sections.title: When the same tendency becomes costly
points: Immediate usefulness does not remove later cost; a key turning point is when you extend preparation into persistent non-participation.
Use downstream effects to distinguish that cost from genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion, not the type label.
paragraphs: Under heavier load, if action waits for certainty, opportunities and relational feedback may shrink. Use a small reversible test to gather reality-based information. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
If action waits for certainty, opportunities and relational feedback may shrink. Use a small reversible test to gather reality-based information.
sections.reflection_question: When did the same strategy recently pass its point of benefit? Record the immediate gain, the later cost, and whether the counterexample—you can take a first step before the picture is complete—would have served the situation better.

sections.lead: The intention may be constructive, yet an effort to protect energy and accuracy can feel distant or withholding.
sections.title: Where intention and impact may diverge
points: Wanting to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn does not ensure that efforts to step back, gather knowledge, and enter later will be understood that way.
Around information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding, separate intention, observable behavior, and impact to create a repair path.
paragraphs: When judgment needs to pause, you may stay clear enough to sort information without being carried by the first emotional signal. A possible cost to check: If action waits for certainty, opportunities and relational feedback may shrink. Use a small reversible test to gather reality-based information.
A coherent analysis can still miss field conditions. Build in observation, conversation, or a practical trial.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks where intent and impact diverged. What did you mean to protect, what did the other person receive, and what clarification might have narrowed the gap?

sections.lead: You may offer insight, solve difficult problems, respect space, and remain dependably available.
sections.title: How care is expressed and what treatment matters
points: Care may be expressed when you step back, gather knowledge, and enter later, but a type cannot specify what the other person needs.
Asking whether support landed also tests whether the aim to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn was central in that moment.
paragraphs: Useful information, steady support, and respect for boundaries may be ways you show care. Check whether availability and emotional contact are visible as well. In conflict, you may focus first on information, boundaries, and available resources. Add one sentence about your current feeling and a time for returning to the conversation.

It may be easier for you to understand that others also need alone time, preparation time, and clear boundaries; this can reduce feelings of oppression, but you still need to let the relationship know when you will respond.
sections.reflection_question: Think of a recent relationship situation that involved distinguishing necessary preparation from delayed participation. How did you express care? Ask whether it landed as support, pressure, or something else. How did the answer differ from your expectation?

sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to retreat as demands for closeness rise and leave the duration of the boundary unclear.
sections.title: Recurring relationship difficulties
points: A relational problem may recur when you extend preparation into persistent non-participation, not only with one particular person.
Boundaries, power, and communication history may explain the conflict better than attention to information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding.
paragraphs: While you are sorting out information, the other person may feel rejected. Give return times and response ranges when space is needed, making boundaries predictable rather than just empty spaces.

Silence, reduced interaction, or time alone may help someone recover attention and organize information, or may mean the topic is not yet workable. State the question and timing clearly, then allow a bounded interval before following up.
sections.reflection_question: Which relationship difficulty recurs with different people? Where did you need to distinguish necessary preparation from delayed participation, and what was better explained by boundaries, power, or communication habits?

sections.lead: Conflict may escalate when you detach from emotion and analyze, then cut contact if pressure continues.
sections.title: How conflict escalates and how repair can begin
points: As conflict escalates, concern with information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding may crowd out feelings and the shared aim.
Repair turns the wish to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn into a bounded request rather than a personality judgment.
paragraphs: In conflict, you may focus first on information, boundaries, and available resources. Add one sentence about your current feeling and a time for returning to the conversation.
It's not that I don't care. I need some time to sort it out and will come back before tonight to respond to this matter.
sections.reflection_question: Review one conflict in which you needed to distinguish necessary preparation from delayed participation. What was the first observable signal, and where could repair begin with facts, feelings, and a bounded request?

sections.lead: In task settings, you may tend to understand the system, dependencies, and information quality before choosing a high-leverage contribution.
sections.title: How tasks move and the conditions that help
points: The tendency to step back, gather knowledge, and enter later can support quality or pace at the right task stage.
As the stage changes, reassess whether investment in information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding still fits.
paragraphs: At work, your attention may go first to information quality, system structure, the basis for judgment, and reusable knowledge. This does not establish job fit, competence, or performance.
When the requirements are complex, the information is noisy, or the argument lacks basis, it may be easier for you to break the chaotic information into structures, variables, and hypotheses.
sections.reflection_question: During a task stage when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, how did this way of working improve quality or pace? At what later stage did it need to be complemented by a different strategy?

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may bring depth but work best with explicit requests, preparation time, and clear sharing boundaries.
sections.title: Information, feedback, and friction in collaboration
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion.
paragraphs: In meetings without background material, thinking time, or problem boundaries, you may be more likely to be tense and your output may be conservative. You can ask for topics, decision points and acceptable answer depth in advance, or give a three-level response of "preliminary judgment, information to be verified, and next step confirmation".
Letting you read the background first is more effective than asking questions on the spot.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration where you needed to distinguish necessary preparation from delayed participation, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?

sections.lead: Around authority, you may prefer autonomy and expertise when leading and need space plus evidence-based feedback when led.
sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to extend preparation into persistent non-participation.
paragraphs: When you are in a design, gatekeeping, or interpretation position, influence may come from sorting out the underlying logic, architectural dependencies, knowledge base, and decision-making basis to make complex problems more understandable. It indicates the cognitive organizational style and does not equal the conclusion of leadership ability, decision-making authority or job fit.

When others need your judgment or solution, giving the background, problem boundaries, purpose and preparation time in advance may make your output clearer. It indicates information processing preferences and does not mean that you cannot participate in rapid collaboration.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?

sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may reduce contact, hoard time and knowledge, and react strongly to unscheduled demands.
sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to step back, gather knowledge, and enter later until it begins to extend preparation into persistent non-participation.
Sleep, workload, and genuine complexity or an actual privacy intrusion must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
paragraphs: The information set keeps growing while the decision or next step remains undefined.
Analysis, data, and models crowd out feelings, constraints, and feedback from the actual situation.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?

sections.lead: With more safety, you may respond in real time, share unfinished thinking, and let others see the working process.
sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases
points: When safety increases, the impulse to step back, gather knowledge, and enter later is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to information, boundaries, resource demand, and complete understanding, not evidence that you have become another type.
paragraphs: You may notice early when attention, time, or energy needs a boundary.
When information and boundaries are sufficient, you may organize complexity into a structure others can examine.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, you can take a first step before the picture is complete? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?

sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to replace endless readiness with small doses of participation and state capacity before disappearing.
sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type
points: Growth adds an optional step before you step back, gather knowledge, and enter later; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can prepare sufficiently without being overdrawn without the familiar cost.
paragraphs: Set an information threshold for one question this week. When you reach it, offer a provisional judgment, name the uncertainty, and take one reversible step.
Use one small action to test the idea instead of refining the model further.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when information is incomplete, privacy is interrupted, or preparation time shrinks, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?

candidates.short_title: Preserves capacity through understanding and boundaries

growth_actions.title: Time-box research and release the draft
growth_actions.instruction: Set a deadline and minimum output format for a task still under research. Release a draft at that time, label unknowns, and stop substituting further collection for output.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record what was known at release, the effect of omissions, and how much feedback-driven revision followed. Identify which extra preparation would actually have mattered.

growth_actions.title: Share one unfinished thought before full preparation
growth_actions.instruction: Before feeling fully prepared, share one developing view with a trusted person. Label it as provisional and specify the kind of feedback you want.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Track tension around incompleteness, the quality of information received, and whether exchange made the view more accurate rather than less controlled.

growth_actions.title: State capacity and availability in advance
growth_actions.instruction: Before energy is depleted, state your available time, present capacity, and next response point. Do not wait for withdrawal or silence to communicate the boundary.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Check whether others adjusted the request, whether recovery became predictable, and whether the limit was clear instead of abruptly closed.

growth_actions.title: Ask one live question instead of modeling alone
growth_actions.instruction: For one complex problem, ask a relevant person a single question before analyzing alone. Target missing information rather than presenting the whole model.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record analysis time saved or added, any false assumption exposed, and whether the resource cost of direct contact matched the forecast.

growth_actions.title: Schedule one brief period of real-time participation
growth_actions.instruction: Schedule one ten-minute instance of live participation each day: speak, work alongside someone, or remain briefly present. Bound the duration and do not immediately compensate with extra isolation.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare predicted and actual energy cost, one piece of information gained, and one reason personal space still mattered. Use both sides to calibrate the boundary.

sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to overall stability, shared pace, friction, and every party’s place.
sections.title: The overall pattern
points: Repeatedly noticing overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace supports this candidate more than one isolated behavior.
If a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation explains the pattern better, a stable type hypothesis deserves less weight.
paragraphs: When many viewpoints coexist, you may first sense the group’s rhythm, the cost of friction, and whether people can stay connected before locating your own position. Gentleness is not the key test; repeatedly placing connection ahead of personal priority is.
Reducing conflict can protect stability while allowing habit to take over postponed choices. Timely preference and action while tension remains would weaken a one-candidate account.
sections.reflection_question: Recall one episode when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance. Where did your attention go first? What supports this candidate, and what points instead to the counterexample that the relationship holds after you state a disagreement?

sections.lead: You may notice overall stability, shared pace, friction, and every party’s place earlier than people around you and allocate effort from there.
sections.title: What draws attention and what you protect

Test that possibility against actual trade-offs while ruling out a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation.
paragraphs: You may first sense whether the whole can keep moving and whether different positions remain compatible before locating your own priority. Conflict cost enters the decision naturally.
The key test is whether personal matters repeatedly disappear when they compete with shared rhythm. Timely preference despite temporary friction is meaningful counterevidence.
sections.reflection_question: In a situation when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, what were you trying hardest to preserve? Which observable consequences help separate useful coordination from lowering your own priority?

sections.lead: The visible move may be to absorb several viewpoints and lower conflict before stating a personal position; the less spoken need may be to know personal priorities can occupy space without creating a crisis.
sections.title: Outer expression and the need beneath it
points: The visible move may be to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position; its purpose still requires contextual and first-person evidence.
Even when the aim is to stay connected while making personal priority visible, another person’s reported impact remains independent evidence.
paragraphs: Under pressure, you may delay taking a position, go along with the situation, mute a preference, return to a familiar routine, or calm the external conflict first. That can stabilize contact, but it can also make your real choice harder to see. This is an observable tendency, not a diagnosis.

A slower pace or delayed position may be heard as procrastination, lack of preference, or silent agreement. Treat that as a communication hypothesis and make your current leaning and return time visible.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance in which someone saw your behavior but may not have understood its purpose. What did you hope to protect, and what alternative explanation did their response add?

sections.lead: A possible habitual sequence is to anticipate friction, postpone a stance, and let unspoken needs become numbness, delay, or passive resistance.
sections.title: How emotion reinforces the habitual loop
points: A loop around overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace narrows through interpretation, emotion, and action rather than appearing all at once.
The pause before you absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position is the point where another response may still be available.
paragraphs: Possible pressure cues include intense conflict, demands for an immediate position, repeated interruption, or the possibility that your preference will create friction. The report cannot determine what you fear or confirm conflict avoidance as a psychological fact.

sections.reflection_question: The last time when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, in what order did emotion, interpretation, and action occur? If you paused at the second step, what different response would still have been available?

sections.lead: A mistyping risk is that coordination roles, courteous restraint, or temporary fatigue can resemble chronic self-deprioritizing.
sections.title: How to recognize the pattern without mistyping
points: Attention to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace across work, relationships, and private choices carries more weight than behavior in one role.
Keep a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation as a serious competing explanation.
paragraphs: You may call silence flexibility even when it postpones a choice you already understand. Ask what you prefer, what friction you are avoiding, and what can be said now at low intensity.

If Nine doesn't emerge as a major clue this time, think of it as a less prominent pattern: Watch to see if you're less proactive in using coordination, noise reduction, and stabilizing rhythms to restore sustainability when the pace is too tight, opinions are scattered, or relationships need buffering. It’s not judging you as inflexible or uncooperative.
sections.reflection_question: When distinguishing useful coordination from lowering your own priority, which evidence repeats across settings, and which similar behavior is better explained by role, culture, temporary strain, or a learned habit?

points: With enough capacity, attention to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace can become a concrete contribution.

sections.lead: When flexibility drops, the same tendency may trade delayed conflict for surface calm until genuine priority becomes hard to locate.
sections.title: When the same tendency becomes costly
points: Immediate usefulness does not remove later cost; a key turning point is when you trade personal priority for immediate ease.
Use downstream effects to distinguish that cost from a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation, not the type label.
paragraphs: Under heavier load, when your preference remains unstated, others have to guess what you want and cooperation loses useful information. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
When your preference remains unstated, others have to guess what you want and cooperation loses useful information.
sections.reflection_question: When did the same strategy recently pass its point of benefit? Record the immediate gain, the later cost, and whether the counterexample—the relationship holds after you state a disagreement—would have served the situation better.

sections.lead: The intention may be constructive, yet an effort to preserve connection can leave others guessing about the decision.
sections.title: Where intention and impact may diverge
points: Wanting to stay connected while making personal priority visible does not ensure that efforts to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position will be understood that way.
Around overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace, separate intention, observable behavior, and impact to create a repair path.
paragraphs: When tension rises, you may help the group slow down enough to keep talking without erasing the disagreement. A possible cost to check: When your preference remains unstated, others have to guess what you want and cooperation loses useful information.
A steady exterior can coexist with depletion, slowing, or avoidance. Treat those changes as cues to make your position visible.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance where intent and impact diverged. What did you mean to protect, what did the other person receive, and what clarification might have narrowed the gap?

sections.lead: You may offer steady presence, acceptance, and room for everyone.
sections.title: How care is expressed and what treatment matters
points: Care may be expressed when you absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position, but a type cannot specify what the other person needs.
Asking whether support landed also tests whether the aim to stay connected while making personal priority visible was central in that moment.
paragraphs: Acceptance, steady presence, and reducing unnecessary friction may be ways you show care. Keep your own preference visible so calm is not mistaken for agreement. In conflict, you may focus first on whether the relationship can remain intact and whether expression will raise the temperature. Add one clear preference or disagreement so stability does not erase your position.
It may be easier for you to maintain companionship and buffering during minor conflicts or rhythm fluctuations.
sections.reflection_question: Think of a recent relationship situation that involved distinguishing useful coordination from lowering your own priority. How did you express care? Ask whether it landed as support, pressure, or something else. How did the answer differ from your expectation?

sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to follow another person’s pace until feeling overlooked becomes silence or stubbornness.
sections.title: Recurring relationship difficulties
points: A relational problem may recur when you trade personal priority for immediate ease, not only with one particular person.
Boundaries, power, and communication history may explain the conflict better than attention to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace.
paragraphs: For the sake of stability, you may not say your preference first, but not saying it for a long time will cause the relationship to lose calibration. Expressing a small preference first is more stable than waiting until you can't bear it and then explode.

Going along, reducing conflict, or delaying a position may keep the relationship workable, or may reflect difficulty locating a personal preference. Offer concrete options and a clear response time instead of escalating pressure for an immediate answer.
sections.reflection_question: Which relationship difficulty recurs with different people? Where did you need to distinguish useful coordination from lowering your own priority, and what was better explained by boundaries, power, or communication habits?

sections.lead: Conflict may escalate when you cool the temperature and avoid the sharp point, then resist indirectly if pressure continues.
sections.title: How conflict escalates and how repair can begin
points: As conflict escalates, concern with overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace may crowd out feelings and the shared aim.
Repair turns the wish to stay connected while making personal priority visible into a bounded request rather than a personality judgment.
paragraphs: In conflict, you may focus first on whether the relationship can remain intact and whether expression will raise the temperature. Add one clear preference or disagreement so stability does not erase your position.
I just said it’s okay, but actually there is a preference. I prefer this option for this reason.
sections.reflection_question: Review one conflict in which you needed to distinguish useful coordination from lowering your own priority. What was the first observable signal, and where could repair begin with facts, feelings, and a bounded request?

sections.lead: In task settings, you may tend to understand system-wide impact and pacing, contributing strongly to integration and continuity.
sections.title: How tasks move and the conditions that help
points: The tendency to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position can support quality or pace at the right task stage.
As the stage changes, reassess whether investment in overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace still fits.
paragraphs: At work, your attention may go first to alignment, sustainable pace, suppressed disagreement, and whether cooperation can continue. This does not establish job fit, competence, or performance.
When multiple parties have split opinions, inconsistent rhythms, or tense relationships, it may be easier for you to keep everyone discussing at the same table.
sections.reflection_question: During a task stage when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, how did this way of working improve quality or pace? At what later stage did it need to be complemented by a different strategy?

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may build consensus but need explicit personal judgment, deadlines, and non-negotiables.
sections.title: Information, feedback, and friction in collaboration
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation.
paragraphs: If you wait for the situation to naturally stabilize, you may miss a critical window and the team may not know your true position. You can set a time point in advance when you must express your stance, and give a low-intensity version first: what do I prefer, what other concerns do I have, and who needs additional information.
You don’t need to explain everything at once, just express the most certain point at the moment.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration where you needed to distinguish useful coordination from lowering your own priority, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?

sections.lead: Around authority, you may coordinate inclusively when leading and need gentle but definite priorities and follow-through when led.
sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to stay connected while making personal priority visible through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
paragraphs: When you're in a position of alignment, influence can come from muting the noise, embracing dissent, and allowing the rhythm to be uninterrupted by mood swings. It prompts integrated influence clues, which does not mean that you are naturally suitable for leadership, nor does it mean that team differences can only be resolved through gentleness in the long term.

When someone needs your opinion, giving the question, context, and alternative expressions in advance may make it easier for your true thoughts to emerge. It indicates a low-pressure expression of preference and does not mean that you lack a stance or can only passively cooperate.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?

sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may shift into secondary tasks, slow action, and appear agreeable while resisting internally.
sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position until it begins to trade personal priority for immediate ease.
Sleep, workload, and a coordination role or a situation that truly needs de-escalation must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
paragraphs: The more an issue requires a position or a difficult choice, the easier it becomes to postpone.
Organizing, scrolling, or low-effort work takes over while the important decision remains untouched.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?

sections.lead: With more safety, you may recognize preferences sooner, decide proactively, and tolerate short-term disagreement.
sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases
points: When safety increases, the impulse to absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to overall stability, other viewpoints, friction cost, and familiar pace, not evidence that you have become another type.
paragraphs: You may bring patience and continuity to work that depends on steady maintenance rather than short bursts of novelty.
You may understand competing positions without requiring yourself to surrender your own.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, the relationship holds after you state a disagreement? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?

sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to occupy space promptly while preserving connection through small, explicit choices.
sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type
points: Growth adds an optional step before you absorb disagreement, lower tension, and postpone a position; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can stay connected while making personal priority visible without the familiar cost.
paragraphs: In one small decision this week, state your preference, your reason, and what remains negotiable. If you need time, say exactly when you will return to the discussion.
Start with a low-stakes choice and practice making your position visible.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when people move at conflicting speeds, friction appears, or your position may disturb the balance, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?

candidates.short_title: Reduces friction through steadiness and coordination

growth_actions.title: State your preference first in one small decision
growth_actions.instruction: Each day, state your preference first in one small decision, including the option and timing, before hearing others. Do not withdraw it with “anything is fine.”
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record response time, the other person’s actual reaction, and the final choice. Test whether difference truly damaged connection.

growth_actions.title: Put the most important task in the first work block
growth_actions.instruction: Place the most important task in the first available block and close one habitual activity before starting. Require only a minimum advance rather than the right overall mood.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare progress, reduction in routine activity, and energy. Identify the trigger that most often removes the priority from view.

growth_actions.title: Set a firm deadline for one delayed decision
growth_actions.instruction: For one delayed decision, set a date, required information, and a default option at expiry. Once information is sufficient, do not use further coordination to postpone choice.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether the deadline held, the cost of delay, and unresolved disagreement. Allow only one replacement date with a written reason.

growth_actions.title: Restate what you genuinely agree to before saying yes
growth_actions.instruction: Before agreeing, repeat what you will own, what you will not own, and what the other person must carry. Wait for confirmation before beginning.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Check whether the commitment stayed clear, whether resentment or forgetting decreased, and whether you expanded scope merely to restore harmony.

growth_actions.title: Record one disagreement that the relationship survived
growth_actions.instruction: Track the twenty-four hours after voicing one disagreement: the response, relationship change, and issue progress. Do not use immediate tension to predict permanent rupture.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare expected and actual consequences, keeping evidence of continued stability alongside facts that require repair or a renewed boundary.

sections.lead: If this candidate fits, attention may repeatedly return to standards, responsibility, and what could be improved.

paragraphs: With more capacity and choice, when you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding.
When you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding.
sections.reflection_question: In one situation when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws where you still had enough capacity, whom did this attention pattern help and what problem did it solve? Which condition made it a resource rather than an automatic response?

sections.lead: When flexibility drops, the same tendency may promote preferences into principles and keep everyone under continuous review.
sections.title: When the same tendency becomes costly
points: Immediate usefulness does not remove later cost; a key turning point is when you turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
Use downstream effects to distinguish that cost from role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework, not the type label.
paragraphs: Under heavier load, even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect. This is an observation cue, not a level assignment or diagnosis.
Even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.
sections.reflection_question: When did the same strategy recently pass its point of benefit? Record the immediate gain, the later cost, and whether the counterexample—you can stop naturally when the stakes are low—would have served the situation better.

sections.lead: The intention may be constructive, yet an attempt to protect quality can land as criticism or distrust.
sections.title: Where intention and impact may diverge
points: Wanting to act with integrity and dependable standards does not ensure that efforts to check the rule and correct the problem will be understood that way.
Around deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps, separate intention, observable behavior, and impact to create a repair path.
paragraphs: When you explain what a standard protects—quality, fairness, or safety—others can understand your persistence as stewardship rather than fault-finding. A possible cost to check: Even when the work is sufficient, you may feel pulled to add more effort. Separate high-consequence risks from details that can safely remain imperfect.
If the first message is what needs fixing, others may miss the care behind it. State the shared aim before the correction.
sections.reflection_question: Choose an interaction when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws where intent and impact diverged. What did you mean to protect, what did the other person receive, and what clarification might have narrowed the gap?

sections.lead: You may show care through reliability, careful follow-through, and fixing what could cause harm.
sections.title: How care is expressed and what treatment matters
points: Care may be expressed when you check the rule and correct the problem, but a type cannot specify what the other person needs.
Asking whether support landed also tests whether the aim to act with integrity and dependable standards was central in that moment.
paragraphs: Reliability, remembering details, and repairing problems may be ways you express care. Check whether the other person experiences those actions as support, correction, or both; type theory cannot infer either person’s needs. In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
In a relationship with clear agreements and clear responsibilities, it may be easier for you to show that you care by being punctual, honoring your obligations, and handling problems cleanly.
sections.reflection_question: Think of a recent relationship situation that involved distinguishing material risk from personal preference. How did you express care? Ask whether it landed as support, pressure, or something else. How did the answer differ from your expectation?

sections.lead: A recurring relationship difficulty may be to revisit who was responsible and what would have been fair or appropriate.
sections.title: Recurring relationship difficulties
points: A relational problem may recur when you turn low-stakes preferences into principles, not only with one particular person.
Boundaries, power, and communication history may explain the conflict better than attention to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps.
paragraphs: You may be protecting quality or fairness, but if it's an issue right from the start, the other person may feel negated at first. First ask the other person if they are willing to listen to feedback, and then explain the impact of your concerns; repair in the relationship also requires the other person to be willing to respond, rather than just relying on you to make the standards clearer.

Repeated questions about rules, timing, or commitments may be an attempt to make the relationship dependable, but the immediate situation may also carry real risk. Ask which consequence matters most before interpreting the questions as criticism.
sections.reflection_question: Which relationship difficulty recurs with different people? Where did you need to distinguish material risk from personal preference, and what was better explained by boundaries, power, or communication habits?

sections.lead: Conflict may escalate when you enter through facts and principles, then sound increasingly like a verdict when urgency rises.
sections.title: How conflict escalates and how repair can begin
points: As conflict escalates, concern with deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps may crowd out feelings and the shared aim.
Repair turns the wish to act with integrity and dependable standards into a bounded request rather than a personality judgment.
paragraphs: In conflict, you may begin with facts, standards, and what needs to change. Add your feelings, the other person’s perspective, and the actual stakes so the discussion does not collapse into a verdict about who is right.
I just seemed to be finding fault. In fact, what I was worried about was how this incident would affect the next steps. Let me explain the impact clearly first.
sections.reflection_question: Review one conflict in which you needed to distinguish material risk from personal preference. What was the first observable signal, and where could repair begin with facts, feelings, and a bounded request?

sections.lead: In task settings, you may tend to define the standard, material risk, and completion criteria before moving steadily.
sections.title: How tasks move and the conditions that help
points: The tendency to check the rule and correct the problem can support quality or pace at the right task stage.
As the stage changes, reassess whether investment in deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps still fits.
paragraphs: At work, your attention may go first to standards, process gaps, ownership, and acceptable quality. This can explain why calibration matters to you, but it does not establish competence, job fit, or performance.

When requirements, acceptance criteria or delivery standards are still vague, it may be easier for you to break them into checklists, process nodes and review questions to help the team reduce rework.
sections.reflection_question: During a task stage when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, how did this way of working improve quality or pace? At what later stage did it need to be complemented by a different strategy?

sections.lead: In collaboration, you may value dependable handoffs and closed loops, with low tolerance for ambiguous ownership.
sections.title: Information, feedback, and friction in collaboration
points: Collaboration can strain when concern with deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps is not translated into usable information and feedback.
Repair goals, ownership, and communication design before ruling out role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework.
paragraphs: When you are quick to point out omissions, discrepancies, or inconsistencies, collaborators may first hear "being corrected" rather than hearing that you are protecting the quality of your delivery. A more negotiable approach is to first explain the risks, acceptance criteria, or common goals associated with this piece of feedback, and then distinguish between the parts that must be corrected and those that can be observed later; this is just a clue to communication friction, and it does not mean that you are necessarily picky or that others are necessarily resistant to feedback.
By explaining the risks, impacts, and shared goals before asking a question, you reduce the chance that others will interpret your warning as critical.
sections.reflection_question: In a recent collaboration where you needed to distinguish material risk from personal preference, was the missing ingredient information, feedback design, ownership, or psychological safety? What evidence shows that type need not explain it?

sections.lead: Around authority, you may over-check when leading and seek explicit standards and rationale when being led.
sections.title: Leading and being led: authority, boundaries, and interaction
points: Clear authority makes it less necessary to act with integrity and dependable standards through guessing or repeated escalation.
Explicit decision rights and stopping conditions help prevent the pattern from starting to turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
paragraphs: When you are in a leading, coordinating or reminding position, your influence may come from clarifying goals, standards, responsibilities and review mechanisms, so that delivery does not rely solely on personal awareness. It is suitable for use in scenarios where quality risks are high and processes are prone to drift; however, this only affects style cues and does not mean that the system determines that you have leadership capabilities or are suitable for management positions.

When others need to collaborate with you, assign tasks, or make requests, it may be easier to keep you engaged by clearly stating boundaries, priorities, acceptance criteria, and where trial and error are allowed. What is described here is a preference for collaboration. It is not a general prescription for management methods, nor does it necessarily mean that you need a high-control environment.
sections.reflection_question: In delegating, leading, or being managed when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, which authority or stopping condition remained unclear? What observable outcome would change if it were explicit?

sections.lead: As pressure rises, you may narrow acceptable options, magnify defects, and reduce tolerance for mistakes.
sections.title: How the habit intensifies or changes under pressure
points: Pressure may amplify the impulse to check the rule and correct the problem until it begins to turn low-stakes preferences into principles.
Sleep, workload, and role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework must be checked alongside a type hypothesis.
paragraphs: A minor issue begins to feel urgent before its actual impact has been checked.
After finishing, your attention stays on the remaining gaps rather than what already meets the requirement.
sections.reflection_question: As pressure rose when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, which action intensified first? What did it protect, when did it narrow choice, and could sleep, workload, or real risk explain it better?

sections.lead: With more safety, you may allow several sound approaches and make room for ease without treating it as negligence.
sections.title: What becomes possible when safety increases
points: When safety increases, the impulse to check the rule and correct the problem is no longer the only familiar response.
Look for flexibility while attending to deviation, ownership, and correctable gaps, not evidence that you have become another type.
paragraphs: With enough authority and resources, you may translate problems into clearer processes, documentation, or review practices rather than stopping at criticism.
Your caution can be valuable when safety, commitments, or long-term trust are at stake. In lower-risk situations, distinguish necessary standards from extra effort.
sections.reflection_question: When you felt safe and unhurried, did a different response appear—for example, you can stop naturally when the stakes are low? How could you tell that safety, rather than a different task, accounted for the change?

sections.lead: Growth can mean learning to separate non-negotiable principles from preferences and practice responsible sufficiency.
sections.title: Growth means adding choice, not becoming another type
points: Growth adds an optional step before you check the rule and correct the problem; it does not require erasing the original tendency.
Use seven days of evidence to test whether the new choice can act with integrity and dependable standards without the familiar cost.
paragraphs: For one non-critical task this week, define the minimum acceptable standard, the risks that truly need protection, and the details that may remain unfinished. Review the factual outcome without turning every flaw into a judgment about yourself.
Log the other issues without fixing them immediately, then see which ones still matter the next day.
sections.reflection_question: The next time when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, what small choice could you add without discarding your existing strength? What behavioral evidence after seven days would count as useful?

sections.lead: The following nine editorial observation examples focus on standards, responsibility, and what could be improved for Type 1, The Reformer. They help compare expressions across changes in capacity and pressure. They do not reproduce the theory's nine developmental levels and cannot be assigned from this score.

All nine are observation examples, not system-assigned levels
Scores do not establish health, maturity, or clinical status
paragraphs: These examples compare specific expressions; they are not health grades, diagnoses, or rankings of personal worth.
Use concrete behavior, duration, contextual resources, and counterexamples, and seek appropriate professional support when needed.
sections.reflection_question: While reading these observation examples, what evidence would help distinguish material risk from personal preference? What longitudinal, cross-setting evidence is still missing, so these examples cannot establish health, maturity, or a fixed type?

sections.lead: Early signals may include a stream of “shoulds,” a tightened jaw, or silent rework.
sections.title: Early signals and routes back to choice
points: When you first begin to turn low-stakes preferences into principles, bodily, behavioral, and relational signals often arrive before the later explanation.
Recovery restores choice while checking whether role accountability or a realistic need to prevent rework still requires practical or professional support.
paragraphs: Start by separating critical risks from non-critical imperfections. Choose one low-stakes detail to leave alone, then compare the actual outcome with what you predicted.
Sort issues by consequence, then address only the deviation that most affects the outcome.
sections.reflection_question: For moments when standards slip, ownership is vague, or a deliverable still contains flaws, name one bodily, one behavioral, and one relational early signal. Which low-cost recovery step comes first, and when would another form of support be appropriate?

candidates.short_title: Calibrates reality through standards and responsibility

growth_actions.title: Correct one material issue and defer the rest
growth_actions.instruction: Choose a reversible task with several visible flaws. Rank them by material risk, correct only the first, place the rest on tomorrow’s list, and stop at the criterion set in advance.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Record whether deferred issues caused harm, how long delivery took, and whether physical tension eased after stopping. If material risk grew, revise the risk rule instead of forcing the exercise.

growth_actions.title: Ask what risk the other person sees before stating the standard
growth_actions.instruction: Before stating a standard, ask what risk the other person sees and summarize the answer in one sentence. Then separate required correction from personal preference.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Note any information you had missed, whether the discussion reached a shared standard sooner, and whether you still expressed the boundary clearly.

growth_actions.title: Define “good enough” for one low-risk task
growth_actions.instruction: Before a low-risk task, define minimum acceptance, one risk that must be controlled, and two details that may remain unfinished. Deliver when those conditions are met without raising the bar afterward.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Compare the written standard with the outcome, any rework, and whether others could use the result. Mark which feared imperfections never became consequential.

growth_actions.title: Observe one acceptable outcome after choosing not to correct immediately
growth_actions.instruction: Leave one safe, repairable imperfection untouched for twenty-four hours. Record each urge to correct it and the reason without suppressing the discomfort.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: After twenty-four hours, check the actual consequence, attention consumed, and other people’s responses. If the issue mattered, document the evidence rather than calling the exercise a failure.

growth_actions.title: Turn one criticism into a specific request
growth_actions.instruction: Take one recent criticism and rewrite it as an observable fact, its impact, and a bounded request. Leave room for a response without adding a moral judgment.
growth_actions.observable_outcome: Keep the original and revised versions, then note whether the request could be answered, whether conflict intensity changed, and whether it addressed a material risk.

content.methodology_copy: FC144 二选一迫选版通过成对选择记录两难取舍中的相对动机线索，可作为接近型辨析后的另一份观察材料。两种题型处在同一证据层级，FC144 不替代 E105 的主候选、前三候选或原始计分事实；结果应按 FC144 自身题型边界阅读，不能把跨题型差异解释为人格变化或测评优劣。
content.score_space_boundary: E105 与 FC144 属于同一九型解释框架，但题型、作答任务、计分来源和误差结构不同，不处在同一计分空间。结果页可以复用结构和安全边界；历史、分享、PDF 与重测入口必须保留各自题型来源。页面不直接比较两套数值高低，也不把跨题型的前三候选差异解读成个体状态变化、人格发展或谁更真实。

pages.title: 接下来如何观察自己

actions.title: 每天在一个小决定中先说自己的偏好
actions.instruction: 每天在一个小决定中先说自己的偏好，再听别人意见；偏好要具体到选项和时间，不用“都可以”收回。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录表达所用时间、他人实际反应和最终选择，检验分歧是否真的破坏关系。

actions.title: 把最重要任务放到当天第一个时间块
actions.instruction: 把当天最重要任务放进第一个可用时间块，开始前关闭一项惯性活动。只要求完成最小推进，不等待整体状态合适。
actions.observable_outcome: 比较关键任务的进展、惯性活动减少量和精力变化，找出最容易让优先级消失的触发点。

actions.title: 为一次延期决定设下明确截止点
actions.instruction: 为一个正在拖延的决定设定日期、所需信息和到期后的默认选项。信息足够后不再用继续协调延后选择。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录截止是否兑现、延迟成本和仍未解决的分歧；若需要延期，只接受一个写明原因的新日期。

actions.title: 在同意前复述自己真正愿意承担的部分
actions.instruction: 答应之前先复述自己愿意承担的范围、无法承担的部分和需要对方负责的事项，等待对方确认后再行动。
actions.observable_outcome: 核对承诺是否更清楚、后续怨气或遗忘是否减少，以及你有没有为了恢复和气而扩大范围。

actions.title: 记录一次表达分歧后关系仍然稳定的经历
actions.instruction: 记录一次表达不同意见后的二十四小时：写下对方反应、关系变化和问题进展，不用当下紧张预测长期破裂。
actions.observable_outcome: 比较预期后果与真实后果，保留关系仍稳定的证据，也记录需要修复或重新谈边界的事实。

actions.title: 一次分歧中先问完三个问题再表态
actions.instruction: 下一次分歧中先问完三个问题：对方看到什么、担心什么、希望谁决定。听完后再表达立场，不用问题暗藏反驳。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录三个回答中出现的新信息、你的强度变化，以及延后表态是否真的削弱了边界。

actions.title: 明确说出愤怒下面正在保护的需要
actions.instruction: 感到愤怒时，用一句话说出正在保护的对象或需要，再提出一个有限要求；不把强度当作要求正当性的证明。
actions.observable_outcome: 核对对方能否复述需要、要求是否可执行，以及愤怒下面是否还有受伤、害怕或无力。

actions.title: 把一个可逆决定交给他人负责
actions.instruction: 选择一个后果可逆的决定，写清目标、权限和升级条件后交给他人负责。在约定检查点前不接管过程。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录负责人采取的不同做法、你想介入的次数和最终结果，区分真实风险与控制习惯。

actions.title: 邀请最不同意自己的人先发言
actions.instruction: 会议开始时邀请最不同意你的人先发言，并要求对方给出事实和方案；你只做澄清记录，最后再回应。
actions.observable_outcome: 检查异议是否提前暴露风险、其他人发言量是否变化，以及你的最终决定是否因此更完整。

actions.title: 记录一次降低强度后信息反而更多的场景
actions.instruction: 在一次可控冲突中把音量、语速或结论强度降低一级，明确边界但不追加压迫性理由。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录信息量、对方防御程度和决定质量是否改变；若边界被继续侵犯，说明升级的具体依据。

actions.title: 情绪复杂时仍完成一个十五分钟小步骤
actions.instruction: 情绪复杂时选择一个十五分钟可完成的具体步骤，计时开始，在结束前不等待“更对的感觉”。完成后再决定是否继续。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录开始前后的情绪强度、实际完成物和真实性是否真的受损；若情绪涉及安全风险，优先寻求支持。

actions.title: 记录一件普通但真实满足的事
actions.instruction: 每天记下一件普通但真实满足的事，只写发生了什么、身体怎样回应，不通过比较证明它特别。
actions.observable_outcome: 到 Day 7 查看哪些满足能够重复、哪些只在被认可时出现，并保留一天“没有明显满足”的记录。

actions.title: 向可信任的人提出具体理解请求
actions.instruction: 向可信任的人提出一个可回答的理解请求，例如复述你最在意的部分；不要要求对方完整感受你的全部经验。
actions.observable_outcome: 核对对方是否理解了具体部分、你是否及时纠正误会，以及有限理解能否支持下一步连接。

actions.title: 把比较对象改写为自己真正重视的需要
actions.instruction: 出现比较时，写下羡慕或失落指向的具体需要，再选一个十分钟内能为该需要做的动作，不继续浏览比较材料。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录比较强度是否改变、动作是否真正接近需要，以及哪次比较只是提供信息而没有阻塞行动。

actions.title: 为一段强烈感受同时写下三个事实
actions.instruction: 为一次强烈感受同时写下三个可核实事实、一个身体信号和一种不同解释。二十分钟后再读，不删除原感受。
actions.observable_outcome: 比较原叙事与补充信息，记录行动冲动是否变化；若事实仍支持原判断，就保留边界而不是强迫自己乐观。

steps.prompt: 今天只选一个让你明显紧起来、想推进、想解释、想靠近、想控制或想退开的场景。先写发生了什么和你做了什么，不急着分析号码。
回看今天一个不舒服的瞬间：你当时更在意正确、认可、被需要、安全、边界、自由、真实表达，还是平静？只选最贴近的一项，并写一句证据。
不用给自己定型。只回看前三天：哪一类动机在线索里出现得稍多一点？如果不清楚，就选不清楚，并写下一个可回看的真实场景。
今天观察压力上来后的第一步：迎战、解释、撤退、讨好、转移、控制、麻木、找人确认，还是别的？只记录第一步和后来怎么恢复。
选一段轻微关系摩擦，记录你当时更想被理解、被认可、边界被尊重、得到承诺、被需要，还是让局面平下来。只写自己的需要和行为。
今天只观察一个不太自然出现的资源：求助、拒绝、表达愤怒、放松享受、承认需要、建立规则、主动展示、停下来感受，或承担冲突。
回看这一周，不问哪个号码更好，只问哪些解释更贴近日常动机。可以选择 第一候选、第二候选、前三候选、其他或仍不确定，并写一句可回看的证据。

content.methodology_copy: FC144 二选一迫选版通过成对选择记录两难取舍中的相对动机线索，可作为接近型辨析后的另一份观察材料。两种题型处在同一证据层级，FC144 不替代 E105 的主候选、前三候选或原始计分事实；结果应按 FC144 自身题型边界阅读，不能把跨题型差异解释为人格变化或测评优劣。
content.score_space_boundary: E105 与 FC144 属于同一九型解释框架，但题型、作答任务、计分来源和误差结构不同，不处在同一计分空间。结果页可以复用结构和安全边界；历史、分享、PDF 与重测入口必须保留各自题型来源。页面不直接比较两套数值高低，也不把跨题型的前三候选差异解读成个体状态变化、人格发展或谁更真实。

actions.title: 每天在一个小决定中先说自己的偏好
actions.instruction: 每天在一个小决定中先说自己的偏好，再听别人意见；偏好要具体到选项和时间，不用“都可以”收回。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录表达所用时间、他人实际反应和最终选择，检验分歧是否真的破坏关系。

actions.title: 把最重要任务放到当天第一个时间块
actions.instruction: 把当天最重要任务放进第一个可用时间块，开始前关闭一项惯性活动。只要求完成最小推进，不等待整体状态合适。
actions.observable_outcome: 比较关键任务的进展、惯性活动减少量和精力变化，找出最容易让优先级消失的触发点。

actions.title: 为一次延期决定设下明确截止点

actions.observable_outcome: 记录截止是否兑现、延迟成本和仍未解决的分歧；若需要延期，只接受一个写明原因的新日期。

actions.title: 在同意前复述自己真正愿意承担的部分
actions.instruction: 答应之前先复述自己愿意承担的范围、无法承担的部分和需要对方负责的事项，等待对方确认后再行动。
actions.observable_outcome: 核对承诺是否更清楚、后续怨气或遗忘是否减少，以及你有没有为了恢复和气而扩大范围。

actions.title: 记录一次表达分歧后关系仍然稳定的经历
actions.instruction: 记录一次表达不同意见后的二十四小时：写下对方反应、关系变化和问题进展，不用当下紧张预测长期破裂。
actions.observable_outcome: 比较预期后果与真实后果，保留关系仍稳定的证据，也记录需要修复或重新谈边界的事实。

actions.instruction: 下一次分歧中先问完三个问题：对方看到什么、担心什么、希望谁决定。听完后再表达立场，不用问题暗藏反驳。
actions.observable_outcome: 记录三个回答中出现的新信息、你的强度变化，以及延后表态是否真的削弱了边界。

actions.title: 明确说出愤怒下面正在保护的需要
actions.instruction: 感到愤怒时，用一句话说出正在保护的对象或需要，再提出一个有限要求；不把强度当作要求正当性的证明。
actions.observable_outcome: 核对对方能否复述需要、要求是否可执行，以及愤怒下面是否还有受伤、害怕或无力。

actions.title: 把一个可逆决定交给他人负责

actions.observable_outcome: 记录负责人采取的不同做法、你想介入的次数和最终结果，区分真实风险与控制习惯。
